summary: This informational document describes using static-static Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman with CMS. Both parties use long-term values from certificates, so sender and receiver derive a shared key without extra ephemeral values.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people both have permanent keys, and by combining them they get the same secret without needing temporary ones.

subtitle: Long-term key agreement for encrypted, authenticated, and authenticated-encrypted messages

tldr.problem: CMS structures need a way to establish shared encryption keys between sender and receiver. Ephemeral-static ECDH exists, but does not provide sender authentication.
tldr.mechanism: Both the sender and receiver use their long-term elliptic curve public keys from certificates to derive a shared key-encryption key using ECDH, then use that key to wrap the symmetric key protecting the content.
tldr.outcome: Senders can authenticate themselves through their certified keys, and recipients can be assured the sender possesses the corresponding private key. The approach is now available for EnvelopedData (confidentiality), AuthenticatedData (authenticity), and AuthEnvelopedData (both).

facts.label: Motivation
facts.value: ECMQV removed from NSA Suite B

today: RFC 6278 is an Informational RFC that remains current. It describes how to use static-static ECDH for CMS when ECMQV is unavailable. The specification has been implemented in various cryptographic libraries and security products.

sections.title: Static-Static Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman
sections.content:
Static-static ECDH is a variant of the Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman key agreement scheme where both the sender and receiver use static (long-term) public key values instead of generating fresh ephemeral values for each message. These static values are stored in certificates issued by a certification authority.

In traditional ephemeral-static ECDH, the sender generates a new temporary key pair, sends the public part with the message, and the receiver uses it along with their long-term key to compute the shared secret. This approach does not authenticate the sender. Static-static ECDH improves this by having both parties use certified long-term keys, which implicitly authenticates the sender: only someone possessing the sender's private key could compute the shared secret.

This document specifies how to use static-static ECDH with the three main CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) content types: EnvelopedData, AuthenticatedData, and AuthEnvelopedData.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of each person making a new temporary key every time, they use permanent keys that are already written down in certificates. When they combine these keys, whoever gets the message knows it really came from the person whose name is on that certificate.

sections.title: Diffie-Hellman Variants and CMS Structures
sections.content:
Diffie-Hellman comes in several variants. The original works over modular arithmetic (Z mod p). Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) uses elliptic curve groups, which allow shorter keys with equal security. Within ECDH, there is a choice of standard or cofactor methods; cofactor variant provides additional protection against certain attacks in elliptic curve groups.

Both sender and receiver can use either ephemeral (temporary) or static (long-term) values. This gives four combinations: ephemeral-ephemeral, ephemeral-static, static-ephemeral, and static-static. CMS already supported ephemeral-static for EnvelopedData through RFC 5753, but static-static was missing, especially for the other content types.

CMS defines three main content types for protecting data: EnvelopedData provides confidentiality through encryption; AuthenticatedData provides authenticity and integrity through a Message Authentication Code (MAC); AuthEnvelopedData combines encryption with authentication. This document explains how to use static-static ECDH with all three.
sections.plainLanguage: Diffie-Hellman is a way for two people to create a secret that only they know. You can do it with regular math or with special curve-based math (elliptic curves), and you can make fresh temporary secrets each time or reuse permanent ones. CMS has three types of messages: ones that are locked up, ones that are signed, and ones that are both locked and signed.

sections.title: How Static-Static ECDH Works in CMS
sections.content:
The sending agent first obtains the recipient's certificate, which contains the recipient's static ECDH public key and the elliptic curve parameters. The sender verifies that both their own certificate and the recipient's certificate use the same curve. The sender then chooses whether to use standard or cofactor ECDH, selects a hash function for the key derivation, and optionally creates a unique message-specific value called the ukm (user keying material).

The sender performs the ECDH computation using the two static public keys and their own private key to derive a shared secret. This shared secret is then processed through a key-derivation function (KDF) along with the selected hash algorithm and an optional ukm value. The result is a pairwise key-encryption key (KEK) used to wrap the symmetric key protecting the content.

The receiving agent looks up the sender's certificate based on the information in the message, verifies the curve parameters match their own, and performs the corresponding ECDH computation on their side. Because ECDH is symmetric—both parties compute the same shared secret from their own private key and the other's public key—the receiver derives the same KEK and can unwrap the content-encryption key to access the message.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender looks at the receiver's certificate to get their public key. The sender mixes their own private key with the receiver's public key using special math. The receiver mixes the sender's public key (from their certificate) with their own private key. Both end up with the same secret number. They use this to unlock a key that unlocks the message.

sections.title: Implementation Requirements
sections.content:
All implementations supporting this specification MUST support standard elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman and SHOULD use the curve parameters defined in RFC 5480. The key-agreement algorithm identifier includes the selected hash function (SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512); implementations MUST support at least the SHA-256 variant and SHOULD NOT use SHA-1.

Key wrapping must use AES (Advanced Encryption Standard); implementations MUST support AES-128 wrap and MAY support AES-192 and AES-256. Support for AuthenticatedData and EnvelopedData is RECOMMENDED; support for AuthEnvelopedData is OPTIONAL.

For content encryption, implementations MUST support at least AES-128-CBC and MAY support other modes such as AES-GCM or AES-CCM for authenticated encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: Code that uses this must support the basic version and should use strong hash functions like SHA-256 instead of the older SHA-1. It must be able to wrap keys with AES encryption. Supporting locked messages and signed messages is good; supporting messages that are both locked and signed is optional.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Critical security issue: when using static-static ECDH without a fresh ukm value in every message, the same KEK is reused between the sender and receiver for multiple messages. This is bad cryptographic practice and may expose the system to attacks such as the small-subgroup attack. Message senders SHOULD always include a unique ukm value, typically a random string at least as long as the key-wrap algorithm's key size.

Another important limitation: static-static ECDH with key-agreement does not inherently provide data-origin authentication in all cases. Consider a scenario where an attacker intercepts a message, recovers the KEK, creates new plaintext, re-encrypts it with the same KEK, and replaces the original content. If the message was sent to multiple recipients, the second recipient cannot determine whether the modified content came from the original sender or the attacker. Applications requiring guaranteed data-origin authentication should use digital signatures in addition to key agreement.

Organizations that centrally generate and manage their users' ECDH keys should be aware that their central infrastructure could decrypt communications between their users, unlike with ephemeral-static ECDH where the sender's infrastructure could not decrypt (though the receiver's infrastructure could).
sections.plainLanguage: The biggest risk is if the sender sends two messages with the same secret number—an attacker can trick the system. So always include a fresh random number in each message. Also, even though you know the sender has the key, you don't always know they actually chose the message content—so really important things should have signatures too.
